item.title: China quietly expands economic pressure toolkit during trade truce
item.description:
Even as Washington and Beijing publicly prepare for a mid-May summit between President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping, China has been quietly assembling a broad new arsenal of economic countermeasures under cover of the trade truce the two leaders struck last October in Busan, South Korea.

Since that meeting — which Trump rated "a 12 out of 10" — Beijing has enacted sweeping new laws, tightened export controls on critical minerals, banned foreign AI chips from state-funded data centers, barred American and Israeli cybersecurity software from Chinese firms, and begun weighing restrictions on solar manufacturing equipment exports to the United States, according to a Reuters analysis published on Sunday.

item.title: Iran refuses talks unless US lifts naval blockade
item.description: The US Navy intercepted the sanctioned tanker M/V Sevan in the Arabian Sea on Saturday, forcing the vessel to turn back toward Iran under escort as the American naval blockade of Iranian ports continues to expand. The operation brought the total number of vessels redirected since the blockade began on April 13 to 37.

item.title: Hardliner set to replace Ghalibaf in Iran nuclear talks
item.description: A confidential letter addressed to Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei has exposed a rift at the highest levels of power in Tehran, with senior officials warning that the country's economic crisis leaves no choice but to negotiate with the United States over the nuclear issue — a position that directly challenges a red line set by Khamenei himself.

item.title: Zelenskyy says EU accession talks could open in June
item.description:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Sunday that he expects the European Union to formally open the first negotiating clusters for Ukraine's accession talks as soon as June, declaring that Kyiv has fulfilled all the preparatory requirements demanded by Brussels.

"We see approximate dates, maybe in June," Zelenskyy said, according to Liga.net, adding that a decision on the clusters could come between late May and June. The remarks came after a meeting in Kyiv with Moldovan President Maia Sandu, with both leaders pressing the EU to move forward on membership negotiations without further delay.

item.title: Global military spending hit record $2.89 trillion in 2025, SIPRI reports
item.description: World military expenditure reached $2.887 trillion in 2025, marking the 11th consecutive annual increase and the highest level ever recorded, according to new data released Monday by the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI). The 2.9 percent real-terms increase pushed global military spending to 2.5 percent of GDP, its highest share since 2009.

item.title: Iran war pushes African, South Asian homes back to charcoal and firewood
item.description:
Before sunset in Nairobi's Kibera settlement, Brenda Obare used to cook dinner with a quick turn of her gas stove's knob. Now she crouches over a charcoal burner, coaxing a smoky fire outside her tin-roofed home. "We don't have many options," she told the Associated Press. "You use what you can afford."

Obare's story has become emblematic of a cascading crisis. The war between the United States, Israel, and Iran — which began in late February and led to the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz — has disrupted roughly 20 percent of global oil and liquefied natural gas trade. As energy prices surged more than 55 percent since the conflict began, the shockwaves have reached the kitchens, forests, and wildlife habitats of Africa and South Asia, threatening years of progress in public health and conservation.

item.title: Iran war sends PCB prices surging, squeezing tech firms
item.description: The Iran war's toll on the global tech supply chain deepened this week as Reuters reported that Iran's early April strike on Saudi Arabia's Jubail petrochemical complex has halted production of high-purity polyphenylene ether (PPE) resin, a critical material used to manufacture the printed circuit board laminates found in virtually every electronic device.

item.title: China races to build 2,800-satellite AI network in orbit
item.description: China is pushing forward on two fronts in space — a commercial initiative to build a 2,800-satellite AI computing network and a military expansion that U.S. officials warn could challenge American dominance in orbit within the next decade and a half.

item.title: Trump warns Iran's oil pipelines could explode within three days
item.description: US President Donald Trump warned on Sunday that Iran's oil pipelines could "explode from within" in a matter of days, ratcheting up pressure on Tehran to agree to a ceasefire deal as the two-month-old conflict entered its latest phase of brinkmanship.

item.title: China blocks Meta's $2B acquisition of AI startup Manus
item.description:
China's top economic planner on Monday ordered the cancellation of Meta Platforms' $2 billion acquisition of artificial intelligence startup Manus, a decisive move to keep homegrown AI technology within Beijing's borders amid an intensifying tech rivalry with the United States.

The National Development and Reform Commission issued a brief statement saying the deal's cancellation was made "in accordance with laws and regulations," according to Bloomberg and Reuters. The NDRC did not elaborate further. Meta representatives did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

item.title: Iran's Araghchi meets Putin as US peace talks stall
item.description: Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi arrived in St. Petersburg on Monday to hold talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin, capping an intensive diplomatic tour across Pakistan and Oman as negotiations between Tehran and Washington over the ongoing conflict remain stalled.

item.title: OpenAI, Microsoft end exclusive IP deal in revised pact
item.description: OpenAI and Microsoft disclosed an amended partnership agreement on Sunday that removes Microsoft's exclusive rights to OpenAI's intellectual property and allows the AI company to serve customers across any cloud provider, according to The Wall Street Journal. The revised deal grants OpenAI more freedom while capping the revenue share it must pay Microsoft, marking the latest chapter in a relationship that has grown increasingly complex as the AI industry has expanded.

item.title: Adidas shares rise after sub-two-hour marathon record
item.description:
Shares of Adidas rose on Monday after athletes wearing the company's new Adizero Adios Pro Evo 3 racing shoe delivered a historic performance at the 2026 TCS London Marathon, including the first official sub-two-hour marathon in history.

Kenya's Sabastian Sawe crossed the finish line on Sunday in one hour, 59 minutes and 30 seconds, shattering the previous world record held by the late Kelvin Kiptum by 65 seconds and becoming the first man to break the two-hour barrier in a sanctioned race. Ethiopia's Yomif Kejelcha finished second in 1:59:41, meaning two men ran under two hours in the same competition. In the women's race, defending champion Tigst Assefa set a new women-only world record of 2:15:41, with the top three women all finishing under 2:16 for the first time in marathon history.

All three record-setters wore the Adizero Adios Pro Evo 3. Adidas shares climbed approximately 1.2% on Monday following the results, according to Reuters.

item.title: Chinese scientists unveil iron flow battery and zero-emission coal cell
item.description: Two separate research teams from Chinese institutions have announced advances in clean energy technology this month, proposing a near-zero-emission coal fuel cell and unveiling an iron-based flow battery that could reshape large-scale energy storage.

item.title: Seized Iran-linked supertankers sail west under US control
item.description:
Two Iran-linked oil supertankers seized by U.S. forces in the Indian Ocean last week are now sailing westward in close proximity to each other, according to maritime tracking data, though Washington has given no formal indication of their intended destination.

The M/T Tifani was boarded by U.S. Navy SEALs on April 21 between Sri Lanka and Indonesia, carrying approximately 2 million barrels of Iranian crude loaded at Kharg Island earlier in the month. Two days later, on April 23, U.S. forces boarded the M/T Majestic X — formerly known as the Phonix — in roughly the same stretch of the Indian Ocean. That vessel, a Very Large Crude Carrier also capable of transporting 2 million barrels, had been bound for Zhoushan, China. Both tankers were seized pursuant to warrants issued by the U.S. Department of Justice, according to TankerTrackers.com.

item.title: Merz says US is being 'humiliated' by Iran as talks stall
item.description: German Chancellor Friedrich Merz delivered a pointed rebuke of the United States' strategy in its ongoing conflict with Iran on Monday, warning that Washington lacks a credible path out of the war and that the Iranian leadership is making a mockery of American diplomatic efforts.

item.title: Iran offers to reopen Hormuz as strait traffic grinds to a halt
item.description: The Strait of Hormuz has ground to a virtual standstill, with only a handful of small vessels observed transiting the waterway over the weekend as competing American and Iranian blockades choke off one of the world's most critical shipping lanes. Peace negotiations between Washington and Tehran remain frozen, raising the specter of a prolonged supply disruption affecting crude oil, natural gas, and fertilizers.

item.title: China's clean energy exports shatter records as Iran war reshapes global demand
item.description: The war in Iran has sent oil-starved countries scrambling for alternative energy sources, and many are turning to China, the world's dominant producer of solar panels, batteries, and electric vehicles. New data shows the conflict is accelerating a global shift toward renewables at a pace that has surprised even energy analysts.

item.title: Iran war energy shock drives charcoal surge, threatening African wildlife
item.description:
In Brenda Obare's kitchen in Kibera, one of Nairobi's largest informal settlements, the blue flame of a gas stove has given way to a charcoal fire. "We don't have many choices," she told the Associated Press. "You make do with what you can afford."

Her story is becoming common across Africa and South Asia, where energy disruptions caused by the Iran war are pushing millions of families back to charcoal and firewood as cleaner cooking fuels grow unaffordable. The reversal is threatening years of progress in conservation and public health.

item.title: Iran war and record heat reshape global energy markets
item.description: Two months into the war in Iran, the closure of the Strait of Hormuz and a punishing wave of early-season heat across Asia are reshaping global energy markets, driving record electricity demand and accelerating a shift toward renewable power — with China emerging as the chief beneficiary.
